name: Collagen filler

lead: Collagen fillers are injected into the skin to smooth wrinkles and fold lines and to add lip volume, with the plumping visible right after treatment. Bovine collagen (Zyderm, Zyplast) was the leading filler in the US for about two decades and was long treated as the gold standard.

The injected collagen physically adds volume under a line or fold and is gradually absorbed, so the effect is temporary. Hyaluronic acid fillers have since taken over in many markets, a shift that included a randomised trial comparing Restylane with bovine Zyplast in nasolabial folds. Forum mentions of collagen today mostly concern supplements.

paras: It is injected by clinicians into lines, folds or lips, with repeat treatments needed to maintain the look. Fillers containing bovine collagen involve an allergy screening step beforehand.

Reviews note hypersensitivity reactions with bovine collagen, and the FDA advises allergy screening for fillers containing collagen. As with all fillers, bruising, swelling and lumps can occur, and results are temporary.

angle.text: Collagen filler is the original injectable, used to soften wrinkles and fold lines and to add lip volume, with the plumping visible right after treatment. It is temporary, bovine versions can provoke allergies, and hyaluronic acid has largely replaced it.

lead: Collagen fillers are injectable implants made from animal-derived (chiefly bovine) or human bioengineered collagen, used to soften wrinkles and fold lines and to add soft-tissue volume, so the face looks smoother and fuller without surgery.[1][2] They are generally regarded as the original modern injectable dermal filler: a 2006 review notes that bovine collagen was the most popular injectable implant in the United States for nearly two decades before human bioengineered collagen products and hyaluronic acid fillers became available.[1]

A 2001 review described injectable Zyderm bovine collagen as having come to be regarded as the benchmark against which other fillers were measured.[3] The correction is temporary, and bovine products can cause hypersensitivity reactions, which is the context for a randomised trial comparing hyaluronic acid (Restylane) with bovine collagen (Zyplast) in the nasolabial folds.[4]

Collagen fillers have been largely displaced in many markets by hyaluronic acid, though newer collagen-based and recombinant-collagen products continue to be registered for study.[5][6][7] Forum discussion of collagen as an injectable is sparse; most online mentions of collagen concern dietary supplements and creams, which are a different category from injected implants.[8]
infobox: Temporary; Zyplast phagocytosed by 6 months in one histology study[4][2]
Fillers are regulated as medical devices in the US
Hyaluronic acid fillers in many markets[1][4]

paras: A review of collagen fillers outlines the injectable collagen implants available, including animal- and human-derived types, along with injection techniques, preferred treatment methods and possible adverse reactions.[1] Dermal fillers in general are injectable gels or hydrogels, often made from natural polymers such as hyaluronic acid, collagen or gelatin, or from synthetic polymers, and are used mainly to change facial appearance.[9] Wikipedia notes that glutaraldehyde crosslinking has been used with collagen-based fillers to improve their integration.

Collagen is the main structural protein of skin and connective tissue. Wikipedia's collagen article states that collagen applied to the skin in creams does not penetrate it and that there is little good evidence that eating collagen affects skin health; injected collagen implants work by a different route, physically placing material beneath the skin.[8]

sections.h: How it is used for appearance
paras: Collagen implants are injected into the dermis to lift wrinkles, nasolabial (smile) folds, and other lines or depressions, and to augment soft tissue. The Narins trial treated the nasolabial folds, the creases running from the nose to the corners of the mouth, and the registered studies of newer collagen products target nasolabial folds and crow's feet.[4][5][6] Treatments in the 2003 trial were repeated at two-week intervals as needed to reach an optimal cosmetic result, which illustrates that more than one session could be needed.[4]

Bovine collagen was the dominant injectable in the US for roughly two decades before alternatives appeared, according to a 2006 review.[1] Zyderm, an injectable bovine collagen, was regarded by 2001 as the benchmark filler.[3] Human bioengineered collagen products and hyaluronic acid fillers followed.[1] A 2003 randomised trial compared Restylane, a non-animal stabilised hyaluronic acid, with Zyplast, a cross-linked bovine collagen, marking the period when hyaluronic acid products began to challenge collagen as the standard.[4] Hyaluronic acid is today the most common filler material, typically lasting several months to a year.[9]

The 2003 trial in Dermatologic Surgery randomised 138 patients so that each had hyaluronic acid on one side of the face and bovine collagen on the other. A blinded investigator assessed outcomes at 2, 4 and 6 months. Less hyaluronic acid gel was needed to reach the optimal result, and at six months the hyaluronic acid side was rated superior in 56.9 percent of patients on the Wrinkle Severity Rating Scale and 62.0 percent on the Global Aesthetic Improvement Scale, versus 9.5 and 8.0 percent for collagen; the authors concluded hyaluronic acid gave more durable improvement.[4]

A histology study by Lemperle and colleagues injected ten filler substances into one author's forearm and sampled the sites at 1, 3, 6 and 9 months; it reported that Zyplast collagen was phagocytosed (cleared by immune cells) by six months.[2] The cited trial literature describes bovine collagen as giving temporary correction.[4]

The trial literature describes bovine collagen as capable of causing hypersensitivity reactions.[4] The FDA's dermal filler guidance notes that some fillers contain collagen or egg-derived products and advises that people allergic to collagen tell their provider; it also advises allergy testing before fillers made with certain animal-derived materials. Reviews of collagen substances list allergenicity and adverse reactions among their topics.[3]

For fillers generally, the FDA lists bruising, redness, swelling, pain and itching as common effects, nodules, granulomas, infection and allergic reactions as less common, and accidental injection into a blood vessel as the most concerning complication, capable of tissue death, vision problems including blindness, and stroke. A 2013 review by Funt and Pavicic found that most filler reactions are mild and temporary, that serious events are uncommon, and that complications relate mainly to injection volume and technique, though some relate to the material.[2] The FDA advises against self-injection and against buying fillers online, because products may be counterfeit or unapproved.

In the United States the FDA regulates dermal fillers as medical devices, approving absorbable fillers for adults 22 and older for facial wrinkles and folds and certain lip, cheek, chin and hand augmentation. Regulation elsewhere varies; in the UK and EU a CE mark is required.

Collagen replaced earlier filling approaches for a generation of patients and was the reference product in the 1980s and 1990s market, until hyaluronic acid products, with longer duration and a way to dissolve them, took over in many markets.[1][4][9] Looksmaxxing forum discussion centres on hyaluronic acid, fat grafting, implants and other face-volume options; collagen injection is rarely discussed, and forum mentions of collagen usually concern supplements and peptides.[8]

A randomised, double-blind, multicentre comparison of Restylane with Zyplast for nasolabial folds in 138 patients was published in 2003; hyaluronic acid was rated more durable at six months with similar injection-site reactions.[4] A histology study of ten filler substances in one author's forearm found Zyplast collagen phagocytosed by six months.[2]

Registered studies of collagen-containing dermal products include a trial of a collagen dermal filler with lidocaine for nasolabial folds (240 participants), a phase 3 trial of a collagen filler for crow's feet (260 participants, not yet recruiting), and a premarketing trial of a filler combining hyaluronic acid and recombinant collagen.[5][6][7] A phase 3 comparison of TheraFill with Koken on nasolabial folds (73 participants) is also registered.[10]

lore.intro: Collagen injection receives little dedicated discussion in appearance forums, where collagen usually means supplements; those who mention fillers tend to discuss hyaluronic acid.[8]

claims.claim: Collagen fillers were the gold standard before hyaluronic acid.
Collagen results are temporary and fade within months.
Bovine collagen can cause allergic reactions.
Eating or applying collagen has the same effect as injected collagen.

timeline.event: Klein's review describes Zyderm bovine collagen as the long-standing benchmark injectable filler.[3]
Randomised double-blind trial of Restylane versus Zyplast in 138 patients finds hyaluronic acid more durable at six months.[4]
